name: Conservatism
summary: Conservatism, in the sense its defining sources give the word, is a disposition and a tradition of thought that distrusts abstract political reasoning and revolution, trusting inherited institutions, custom, prescription and prudence, and accepting only gradual, discriminating change. It holds that an enduring moral order and a constant, imperfect human nature limit what politics can achieve, prizes private property, local community, religion and the checks that restrain power, and accepts natural and institutional differences against levelling.
scope: Burkean conservatism as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines the narrow sense: the line from Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France through Coleridge, Oakeshott and Scruton, together with Russell Kirk's own account of its principles. Following the SEP, which says American right-wing thought is largely neo-conservative and libertarian rather than Burkean, it leaves out neo-conservatism, libertarianism, reaction (de Maistre), fascism, and party platforms; where these defining sources are silent on a policy question, the answer is null.

sources.title: Ten Conservative Principles
sources.author: Russell Kirk
sources.usedFor: Kirk's own account of conservative principles: moral order, custom, prescription, prudence, variety, imperfectability, property, local community, restraints on power, permanence and change.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Burke defends an established aristocracy, the House of Lords and a hereditary Crown, and Kirk says orders, classes and inequalities must survive for a healthy society.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Kirk holds that necessary change ought to be gradual and discriminatory, never unfixing old interests at once, which opposes deliberately speeding change despite institutional disruption.

central-planning.rationale: The SEP says conservatives are sceptical of large-scale economic planning because the wisdom of evolved institutions cannot easily be articulated, and Oakeshott opposes planning from blueprints.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Burke makes the state a partnership of the living, the dead and the unborn, so the living cannot simply dissolve inherited traditions, and the SEP quotes Chesterton's democracy of the dead.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Burke rejected the idea that authority rests on an original contract or abstract popular consent, resting it on prescription and tradition.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Burke attacked the French National Assembly for remaking the constitution from abstract principles and held that change should build on inherited institutions.

decide-locally.rationale: Kirk says in a genuine community the decisions most directly affecting citizens are made locally, and that transfer of those functions to centralised authority endangers community.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Burke says God willed the state and its connection with the source of all perfection, while the SEP notes religious belief is not essential to conservatism and Oakeshott was secular.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Burke defends hereditary succession of the Crown as a pledge of the stability of the whole constitution and an inheritance of the people's liberties.

elective-rulers.rationale: Burke rejects a right to choose our own governors and defends hereditary succession of the Crown, so an elected head of state runs against his stated position.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Kirk names equality before a just court of law as one of the only two true forms of equality.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Kirk says the only true forms of equality are equality at the Last Judgment and before a just court of law, and that all other levelling leads to stagnation; Burke says those who attempt to level never equalize.

future-generations.rationale: Burke's partnership extends to those yet to be born, and the SEP reports Scruton's view that conservatism and conservation are two aspects of a single policy of husbanding resources including the environment.

generational-constitutional-review.rationale: Burke rejects a right of each generation to remake government and holds the constitution an inheritance to be transmitted, with improvement by gradual reform.

gradual-change.rationale: Burke held that a state without means of some change lacks the means of its conservation, favoring cautious reform of inherited institutions.

land-redistribution.rationale: Burke condemns the confiscation of church estates and of a single unoffending citizen's goods, and the levelling of property, as tyranny.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Burke and Kirk rest property rights on prescription, inheritance and antiquity, not on continued use, and Kirk lists the right to bequeath property to posterity among the advantages of property.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Burke praised the balance of crown, lords and commons in the British constitution and distrusted pure democracy.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Burke defends the hereditary Crown as part of the established constitution and a security for English liberty.

more-religion-public.rationale: Burke says religion is the basis of civil society and keeps an established church, and Kirk's moral order is the ground of a good society, while the SEP notes religious belief is not essential to conservatism (Oakeshott was secular) and records no view from him on religion's public role.

municipal-property.rationale: Kirk says separating property from private possession makes Leviathan master of all and that private property is the foundation of civilisation.

national-church-status.rationale: Burke declares that the English are resolved to keep an established church, an established monarchy, aristocracy and democracy, and defends the church establishment at length against its French abolition.

national-rebirth.rationale: Kirk says necessary change should be gradual and that nothing in society should ever be wholly new, which opposes a radical rebirth of the nation.

natural-rulers.rationale: Kirk says a healthy society needs honest and able leadership and that natural and institutional differences among people should be preserved.

one-party-rule.rationale: Kirk says a state in which a small group dominates without check is a despotism, and conservatives seek to limit and balance political power.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Attachment to inherited ways of life, place and nation is central to conservatism.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Kirk approves constitutional restrictions, adequate enforcement of the laws and the web of restraints on will and appetite as instruments of freedom and order.

property-franchise.rationale: Burke wants representation to rest on permanent property and education, while the SEP says conservatives such as Disraeli would broaden the suffrage.

property-fundamental.rationale: Burke and later conservatives treat property as a foundation of liberty and social order.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Burke calls religion the basis of civil society and holds that individual reason is a small stock that does better with the inherited bank of the ages, and the SEP calls conservatism sceptical of political reason, though it presents this as scepticism, not a ranking of reason below faith.

religion-illusion.rationale: Burke and Kirk treat religion and an enduring moral order as true foundations of society, not as consolation for material suffering.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Burke justified the 1688 Revolution as a last resort when the king broke the constitution.

restore-past-order.rationale: The SEP separates conservatism from reaction, which restores a lost order, and Kirk favours reasoned and temperate progress while opposing only the cult of Progress.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Kirk calls conservatism the negation of ideology and says public measures should be judged by probable long-run consequences, and Oakeshott describes it as a disposition, not a doctrine.

sacred-nation.rationale: Burke describes the state as a partnership between the living, the dead and the unborn that connects the visible and invisible world, and Kirk calls the body social a spiritual corporation and a community of souls without which life is meaningless.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Preserving inherited institutions is the defining conservative aim; Burke defended prescription and inheritance against sweeping away the old.

say-in-proportion-to-effect.rationale: Kirk says decisions most directly affecting citizens' lives should be made locally by general agreement of those affected.

second-chamber.rationale: Burke defends the House of Lords as a counterpoise to the Commons and condemns voting it useless.

separate-church-state.rationale: Burke resolves to keep an established church and holds that the state is willed by God and tied to the source of all perfection, which is opposed to strict separation.

separated-powers.rationale: Kirk endorses constitutional restrictions and political checks and balances as instruments of freedom and order, and Burke defends a balanced constitution.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Burke rejects the abstract rights of man in favour of rights inherited as a patrimony, and the SEP records his objection to universal rights, though Kirk adds that human nature is constant.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Kirk says prudent change should be gradual, never unfixing old interests at once, and the SEP records Burke's slow reform of inherited institutions.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Burke rejects destroying existing institutions in favour of gradual reform.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Kirk calls for prudent restraints upon power and says unchecked rule is despotism whether monarchical, aristocratic or democratic.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Kirk contrasts conservatives, who recognise an enduring moral order and duties toward the spiritual order, with those who think material needs are the only needs, and Burke makes the state a partnership connecting the visible and invisible world.

state-harmful.rationale: Kirk says anarchy is intolerable and gives way to tyranny, and Burke makes the state a necessary partnership in every virtue.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Burke says man is a religious animal, that atheism is against reason and instinct, and that atheism is no enemy to be called in to improve a religious system, so a state promoting it is opposed.

total-state.rationale: Kirk opposes involuntary collectivism and central administration doing what communities do, and the SEP records Oakeshott's view that civil association is opposed to the modern interventionist state.

traditional-family.rationale: The SEP presents conservatism's organic social vision as putting faith in the family, private property and religion, and Scruton's account stresses family and community as deference to non-state institutions; neither calls the traditional family the foundation of society in so many words.

universal-morality.rationale: Kirk states that moral truths are permanent and human nature a constant, and the SEP notes conservatives do not deny general principles of justice and truth, only that they can be applied by abstraction.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Kirk lists as a conservative principle that the more widespread the possession of private property, the more stable and productive the commonwealth.

missingStatements.text: Inherited institutions and customs deserve respect even when their reasons are not fully understood.
missingStatements.rationale: Burke defended prescription and inheritance against abstract reasoning, and Oakeshott preferred the tried to the untried.

missingStatements.text: Existing property and social ranks should be defended against schemes of radical leveling.
missingStatements.rationale: Burke's Reflections defends property and a mitigated nobility, and the SEP notes acceptance of hierarchy.

missingStatements.text: Each generation holds society's institutions in trust for those who come after it.
missingStatements.rationale: Burke and Kirk both present society as a continuing partnership across generations, in which present members receive and transmit what they inherit.

notes: Rebuilt on rules 7 from three defining sources saved in scratchpad/sources/conservatism/: the SEP entry, Burke's Reflections (volume 4 of the Works) and Kirk's Ten Conservative Principles. The first pass's answers rested mostly on Wikipedia summaries and guesses about contemporary parties; each was kept only where these sources state a position and was otherwise nulled with its reason in the statement's review history. Goldwater's The Conscience of a Conservative was read but not cited, because the SEP treats American right-wing thought as largely neo-conservative and libertarian rather than Burkean, so it is outside the defining sources' scope. Themes searched: economy (property, levelling, confiscation, planning), government (monarchy, hereditary rank, Lords, representation, checks on power, revolution), society and religion (established church, atheism, family, equality), world, ecology (conservation) and technology (change). Burke and Kirk are silent on most economic policy, foreign affairs, criminal justice, gender, immigration and technology questions, so those are null and the uncertainty rule is expected to fail.
